questions.q: A playwright has interviewed forty factory workers. What would Nottage's approach do with the material, as opposed to verbatim theatre?
choices: Perform each worker's exact words, hesitations included
Invent fictional characters and a plot inspired by the interviews, keeping faith with their experience
Discard the interviews and write from imagination alone
Arrange the quotes by importance, most newsworthy first
questions.explain: Nottage writes fiction drawn from long listening; verbatim theatre (Anna Deavere Smith, The Laramie Project) uses real words.

questions.q: Why did Ruined stop being an adaptation of Brecht's Mother Courage?
choices: The interviews showed that the European frame couldn't hold the Congolese women's stories
Brecht's estate refused permission
The director wanted a well-made play instead of epic theatre
Audiences found Brecht's alienation effects too cold
questions.explain: Nottage kept an echo of Mother Courage in Mama Nadi, but the research convinced her to center the women themselves.

questions.q: Sweat opens in 2008 with two young men just out of prison, then moves back to 2000. What does this do?
choices: It creates a cliffhanger before an ad break
It hides the inciting incident until the final scene
It gives the audience dramatic irony, so they watch asking how these people got here
It follows the unity of time
questions.explain: Knowing something went wrong shifts the question from 'what happens?' to 'how?', the question her research was about.

questions.q: A screenwriter's working-class characters exist mainly to suffer and be pitied. What would Nottage's practice suggest?
choices: Give them a save-the-cat moment in the first ten pages
Add more hardship to raise the stakes
Cut their dialogue so the images speak
Give them humor, knowledge, arguments and choices of their own
questions.explain: Nottage is wary of 'poverty porn'; dignity comes from characters who are sharp, funny and acting for themselves.

questions.q: What was distinctive about how Nottage researched Sweat?
choices: She worked only from census data and news reports
She returned to Reading, Pennsylvania, again and again over about two years or more, listening to residents
She recorded interviews and had actors repeat them through earpieces
She adapted a nonfiction book about the steel industry
questions.explain: With director Kate Whoriskey she made repeated trips from 2011; earpieces are Alecky Blythe's verbatim technique.

questions.q: After Sweat, Nottage and Kate Whoriskey made This Is Reading (2017). What was it?
choices: A documentary film about the 2016 election
A sequel play set in a sandwich shop
A multimedia installation in Reading's old railroad station, with residents among the performers
A verbatim transcript published as a book
questions.explain: It gave the research back to the community. The sandwich-shop play is Clyde's (2021).

questions.q: A reporter wants to borrow Nottage's method for a feature about a struggling town. What carries over, and what doesn't?
choices: The long immersion and listening carry over; composites and an invented climax don't
Everything carries over, as long as the piece feels true
Nothing carries over, because plays are fiction
Only the bar setting carries over
questions.explain: Journalism shares her patience and her respect for subjects but can't invent characters or events.

ideas: Interview a community for years, then write fiction: characters inspired by the people you met, not their exact words.
Let your research overturn your premise, even if you set out to adapt a classic play.
Give the story back to the community that told it, with a performance made in their town and with them.
Write working people with dignity, avoiding poverty porn: nobody onstage exists only to suffer.
